name: Front raise
angleNote: Shoulder flexion: 0° = arm by your side, 90° = arm pointing forward at shoulder height.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end (forearm includes the hand). Approximate textbook anthropometry.
segments.massSource: TODO: check against a published anthropometric table (e.g. Dempster's segment parameters as tabulated by Winter)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult. The arm is modelled straight.

strengthCurve.label: Shoulder flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric shoulder-flexion torque vs angle, assumed to fall off as the arm rises. Approximate shape.
strengthCurve.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

muscles.name: Pectoralis major (clavicular head)
muscles.note: Upper chest; assists flexion in the lower and middle range.

muscles.name: Lateral deltoid
muscles.note: Helps more if the arm drifts out to the side.

muscles.name: Upper trapezius
muscles.note: Rotates the shoulder blade upwards as the arm rises.

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Arm by your side. A dumbbell's line of action passes close to the shoulder; a cable from behind already loads the arm.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The free-weight moment arm grows with the sine of the angle.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Arm near horizontal: the dumbbell's moment arm is the full arm length.

variants.name: Standing dumbbell front raise
variants.notes: Torque = m·g·L·sin(angle): zero at the bottom, maximum at shoulder height. Same curve as the lateral raise, in a different plane.

variants.name: Cable front raise (low pulley behind)
variants.notes: Facing away from a low pulley, the cable running between your legs. It already pulls the arm back at the bottom, so the curve is flatter than with a dumbbell.

variants.name: Chest-supported incline front raise (45°)
variants.notes: Leaning face-down on a 45° bench tilts gravity relative to the body. Below 45° gravity helps raise the arm, and the torque keeps rising past shoulder height (outside this range).
